content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein (stir‑fried noodles) and chop suey (a mix of vegetables, meat and noodles) are popular Chinese‑style dishes often served in fast‑casual restaurants. The NS version uses lean meat (such as chicken, turkey or beef) and wheat‑based noodles (item 1505). The dishes are cooked quickly over high heat, preserving the crunch of the vegetables and the aroma of the spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow mein arrived in the United States in the early 20th century and became an icon of Chinese street food.
The term "chop suey" literally means "assorted leftovers" and originally referred to a dish made from whatever ingredients were on hand.
Noodle 1505 is made from wheat flour and has a medium thickness, making it ideal for rapid stir‑frying.
Traditional recipes often include soy sauce, ginger, garlic and sesame oil.
The NS (no soy) variant may omit soy sauce for those with soy allergies.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Lean meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply B1, B2, B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Vegetables such as carrots, cabbage and bell pepper add dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using lean meat and a modest amount of oil keeps the dish relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Ginger, garlic and the vegetables provide antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles contain gluten, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and pre‑made seasoning packets are often high in salt; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: Restaurant preparation may expose the dish to common allergens such as peanuts or shellfish.

items.title: Meat cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure it is cooked to a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically in a deep bowl or plate. Squeeze fresh lime, sprinkle chopped green onion or add chili to taste. For extra crunch, top with toasted nuts such as cashews or peanuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Chow mein or chop suey is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. When reheating, add a splash of oil to restore noodle crispness.
